verses.text: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered,
“If someone ventures to talk with you, will you be grieved? But who can withhold himself from speaking?
Behold, you have instructed many, you have strengthened the weak hands.
Your words have supported him who was falling, You have made firm the feeble knees.
But now it has come to you, and you faint. It touches you, and you are troubled.
Isn’t your piety your confidence? Isn’t the integrity of your ways your hope?
“Remember, now, whoever perished, being innocent? Or where were the upright cut off?
According to what I have seen, those who plow iniquity, and sow trouble, reap the same.
By the breath of God they perish. By the blast of his anger are they consumed.
The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the fierce lion, the teeth of the young lions, are broken.
The old lion perishes for lack of prey. The cubs of the lioness are scattered abroad.
“Now a thing was secretly brought to me. My ear received a whisper of it.
In thoughts from the visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on men,
fear came on me, and trembling, which made all my bones shake.
Then a spirit passed before my face. The hair of my flesh stood up.
It stood still, but I couldn’t discern its appearance. A form was before my eyes. Silence, then I heard a voice, saying,
‘Shall mortal man be more just than God? Shall a man be more pure than his Maker?
Behold, he puts no trust in his servants. He charges his angels with error.
How much more, those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, who are crushed before the moth!
Between morning and evening they are destroyed. They perish forever without any regarding it.
Isn’t their tent cord plucked up within them? They die, and that without wisdom.’

footnotes.content: Eliphaz steps forward—one of Job's friends who has listened to his pain. What a sacred thing, that friends show up and speak, even when their words wound. Sometimes the bravest thing is to say something hard, knowing it may not comfort.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He asks permission, almost sheepishly—yet speaks anyway. We forget how much it costs a friend to break silence about something painful. Eliphaz knows Job may grieve what he's about to say, yet his loyalty compels him forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eliphaz reminds Job of his own strength—all the people he has steadied and counseled. There's both blessing and sharp irony here: your own wisdom once lifted others. Now who lifts you? It's meant to wound, but also to probe whether Job's faith still stands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Your words held people up. You firmed their weak knees. The strength you gave to others—where is it now? Eliphaz wants Job to see that the very wisdom he dispensed should now comfort him. It's a hard mirror, but not cruel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But now you faint. Now you are troubled. The turning point—from strength to feebleness. Job has become the weak one, the falling one. Eliphaz notices, and his observation cuts to the heart: faith that cannot bear its own trial is faith that may not run deep.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eliphaz asks the question plainly: where is your piety now? Where is your integrity? He wants Job to trust that these are still his foundation, still his hope. Not a reassurance, but a challenge to remember who he is beneath the suffering.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Remember—have the innocent ever perished? Have the upright been cut off? This is Eliphaz's core belief: the righteous are preserved; the wicked fall. It's a theology that works until it doesn't, until you meet someone like Job. The verse carries both wisdom and the seed of its own unraveling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those who plow iniquity reap trouble—it's a plain law of sowing and reaping, as ancient as agriculture itself. Eliphaz appeals to what his eyes have seen, what seems proven by experience. He cannot see that Job's suffering does not fit this tidy frame.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God's breath consumes the wicked—His very presence annihilates them. There's grandeur here, and terror. Eliphaz speaks of a God who acts swiftly against sin. But the question hangs: why does such a God let Job suffer, if Job is innocent?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The roaring lion's teeth are broken. Even the fiercest power is brought low. Eliphaz speaks in vivid images—God subdues all strength that opposes Him. It's meant to comfort: your Maker is mightier than any threat you face.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The old lion perishes for lack. Even hunger masters the king of beasts. All flesh is vulnerable, all appetite subject to scarcity. The image speaks to a hard truth Eliphaz wants Job to accept: we are not exempt from the laws that govern creation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A word was brought to him in secret—Eliphaz appeals now to a vision, a whisper received in silence. He is moving from argument to something more intimate: spiritual experience, a word from beyond himself. What follows will be more than logic; it will be claimed revelation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the night's visions, when sleep falls deep, the mind opens to mysteries. Eliphaz describes the liminal moment—between waking and dreaming—where God is said to speak. It's the voice of experience: I have heard something real here, something that changed me.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fear and trembling seized him; his bones shook. The encounter is physical, overwhelming—not a gentle whisper but something that shakes the whole frame. Eliphaz has met something beyond himself, and it unmade him. Awe, not comfort, is the first effect of God's presence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A spirit passed before his face; the hair of his flesh stood up. He cannot see clearly, only sense the Presence—a form, not a face he can know. The verse captures that holy terror when we brush against the transcendent and know ourselves inadequate to comprehend it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: It stood still; silence fell, then a voice spoke. The Spirit's stillness is itself a presence—the pause before revelation. God does not rush to speak; He lets silence settle first, preparing the heart to hear what cannot be unheard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Can mortal man be more just than God? The voice speaks the deepest question: Can you exceed the One who made you? It is not a comfort in the moment, but a realignment—my smallness before His absolute holiness, my confusion before His perfect righteousness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He puts no trust in servants; He charges angels with error. Even the holy are not immune to the scrutiny of God's justice. If even angels fall short, how can we—dust and brief breath—expect to stand without humbling ourselves before His perfection?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: How much more those in houses of clay, foundation in dust, crushed before the moth. The image is brutal: we are so fragile that a mere moth can undo us. Eliphaz, through his vision, wants Job to see: your suffering fits the condition of your creaturely nature.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Between morning and evening they perish, with no one to mark it. Life is swift, and death swift-er. Most of us vanish without witness or remembrance. It's meant as humbling wisdom, yet it also asks: does God see even when we disappear unseen by others?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their tent cord is plucked up, and they die without wisdom. Readers today hear an echo in this verse—how much of what we build and trust will be dismantled, and yet we still live without asking the deepest question: What remains when all our cords are cut? Only faithfulness to One who does not perish.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
